{{Short description|Chance of overcoming the Coulomb barrier}}
[[File:Gamow peak.png|thumb|300x300px|Tunnelling probability (filled curve) as a function of energy. Left-most curve is the Maxwell–Boltzmann factor and right-most curve is Gamow's factor. '&Delta;' indicates the Gamow window - is <math display="inline">\propto T^{5/6}</math> (''T'' is the temperature).]]
The '''Gamow factor''', '''Sommerfeld factor''' or '''Gamow–Sommerfeld factor''',<ref name="yoon">
{{cite journal
  | author = Yoon, Jin-Hee
  |author2=Wong, Cheuk-Yin
  | title = Relativistic Modification of the Gamow Factor
  | date = February 9, 2008
  | arxiv = nucl-th/9908079
  | doi=10.1103/PhysRevC.61.044905
  | volume=61
  | journal=Physical Review C
  |issue=4
 |article-number=044905
 | bibcode=2000PhRvC..61d4905Y
}}</ref> named after physicists [[George Gamow]] and [[Arnold Sommerfeld]], is a probability factor for two nuclear particles' chance of overcoming the [[Coulomb barrier]] in order to undergo nuclear reactions, for example in [[nuclear fusion]]. By [[classical physics]], there is almost no possibility for protons to fuse by crossing each other's Coulomb barrier at temperatures commonly observed to cause fusion, such as those found in the [[Sun]]. In 1927 it was discovered that there is a significant chance for nuclear fusion due to [[quantum tunnelling]].

While the probability of overcoming the Coulomb barrier increases rapidly with increasing particle energy, for a given temperature, the probability of a particle having such an energy falls off very fast, as described by the [[Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution]]. Gamow found that, taken together, these effects mean that for any given temperature, the particles that fuse are mostly in a temperature-dependent narrow range of energies known as the '''Gamow window'''. The maximum of the distribution is called the '''Gamow peak'''.

== Description ==
When two positively charged nuclei approach each other, they are repulsed by the strong [[electric field]] between them – the [[Coulomb barrier]]. In order to undergo a nuclear reaction, the nuclei must quantum-tunnel through the barrier. The probability of this happening is proportional to the following factor:<ref>{{cite web|publisher=Dept. Physics & Astronomy University College London|title=Nuclear reactions in stars|url=https://zuserver2.star.ucl.ac.uk/~idh/PHAS2112/Lectures/Current/Part7.pdf|access-date=2014-11-12|archive-date=2017-01-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170115214447/https://zuserver2.star.ucl.ac.uk/~idh/PHAS2112/Lectures/Current/Part7.pdf}}</ref>
: <math>P_\text{G}(E) \propto e^{-\sqrt{{E_\text{G}}/{E}}},</math>
where <math>E_\text{G}</math> is the Gamow energy
: <math>E_\text{G} \equiv 2 \mu c^2 (\pi \alpha Z_\text{a} Z_\text{b})^2,</math>

where <math>\mu= \frac{m_\text{a} m_\text{b}}{m_\text{a} + m_\text{b}}</math> is the [[reduced mass]] of the two particles.{{efn|Identical (protons, <sub>2</sub>He<sup>2+</sup>):<math display="inline">\frac{1}{2}m, E_G=mc^2(\pi\alpha\cdot(1,4))^2=m(c\pi\alpha)^2\cdot(1,16).</math><math>m_a\gg m_b:\mu\lesssim m_b,</math> cation vs <sub>1</sub>H<sup>1+</sup>}} The constant <math>\alpha</math> is the [[fine-structure constant]], <math>c</math> is the [[speed of light]], and <math>Z_\text{a}</math> and <math>Z_\text{b}</math> are the respective [[atomic number]]s of each particle.

It is sometimes rewritten using the '''Sommerfeld parameter''' {{math|''η''}}, such that
: <math>P_\text{G}(E) \propto e^{-2\pi \eta},</math>
where {{math|''η''}} is a [[dimensionless quantity]] used in [[nuclear astrophysics]] in the calculation of reaction rates between two [[Atomic nucleus|nuclei]]. It is defined as<ref>{{cite book |last1=Rolfs |first1=C.E. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BHKLFPUS1RcC&pg=PA156 |title=Cauldrons in the Cosmos |last2=Rodney |first2=W.S. |publisher=University of Chicago press |year=1988 |isbn=0-226-72456-5 |location=Chicago |page=156}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Breit |first=G. |year=1967 |title=Virtual Coulomb Excitation in Nucleon Transfer |url=http://www.pnas.org/content/57/4/849.full.pdf |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=57 |issue=4 |pages=849–855 |bibcode=1967PNAS...57..849B |doi=10.1073/pnas.57.4.849 |pmc=224623 |pmid=16591541 |access-date=27 January 2015 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

: <math> \eta = \frac{Z_a Z_b e^2}{4 \pi \epsilon_0 \hbar v} = \alpha Z_1 Z_2 \sqrt{\frac{\mu c^2}{2E}},</math>

where {{math|''e''}} is the [[elementary charge]], {{math|''v''}} is the magnitude of the relative incident [[velocity]] in the centre-of-mass frame.{{efn|<math>\eta_{id}=\frac{(1,2)^2e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0\hbar v}=\frac{1}{2}c\alpha\cdot(1,4)\sqrt{\frac{m}{E}}</math>}}

=== ''S''-factor ===
The probability of a nuclear reaction is proportional to the probability that the particles penetrate the barrier <math>P_\mathrm{G}</math>, times the probability that they react upon doing so. The latter probability is described by the '''astrophysical ''S''-factor'''.

The ''S''-factor depends on the complicated [[strong force]] interactions between the nuclei, and thus nonlinearly depends on particle energy. It is defined as<ref>{{cite book |last1=Thompson |first1=Ian J. |last2=Nunes |first2=Filomena M.|author2-link=Filomena Nunes |date=2009 |title=Nuclear Reactions for Astrophysics: Principles, Calculations and Applications of Low-Energy Reactions. |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |page=5 |isbn=978-0-521-85635-5 }}</ref>

: <math>S(E) \equiv \frac{E}{\exp(-2 \pi \eta)} \sigma(E)</math>,

where {{mvar|σ}} is the [[Nuclear cross section|cross section]], a measure of the total reaction probability.

The Coulomb barrier causes the cross section to have a strong exponential dependence on <math>E</math>. The ''S''-factor remedies this by factoring out the Coulomb component of the cross section (the Gamow factor) and the [[Matter wave|de Broglie wavelength]] (the cross section is proportional to the wavelength squared: <math>\lambda^2 = \tfrac{h^2}{2mE}\propto\tfrac{1}{E}</math>). For nuclear reactions without [[Resonance (particle physics)|resonances]], <math>S</math> varies less with <math>E</math> than <math>\sigma</math> does. Thus, <math>S</math> is a useful reparameterization of <math>\sigma</math>.<ref name="atzeni">{{cite book |first1=Stefano |last1=Atzeni |first2=Jürgen |last2=Meyer-ter-Vehn |title=The physics of inertial fusion: Beam plasma interaction, hydrodynamics, hot dense matter |date=2004 |publisher=Clarendon Press |location=New York |isbn=0198562640 |pages=3–14}}</ref>

=== Gamow peak ===
For an [[ideal gas]], the [[Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution]] is proportional to
:<math>P_\text{MB}(E)\propto e^{-m\langle v^2\rangle/2k_{\rm B}T}=e^{-E/k_{\rm B}T}</math>
where <math>\langle v^2 \rangle</math> is the average squared speed of all particles, <math display="inline">k_{\rm B}</math> is the [[Boltzmann constant]] and ''T'' is absolute temperature.

The fusion probability is the product of the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution factor and the Gamow factor
:<math>P_\text{fusion}(E)=P_\text{MB}(E)\cdot P_\text{G}(E) \propto \exp\left(-\frac{E}{k_\mathrm{B}T}-\sqrt{\frac{E_{\rm G}}{E}}\right)</math>
The maximum of the fusion probability is given by <math display="inline">\partial P_\text{fusion}/\partial E=0, </math> which yields<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Clayton |first=D. D. (Donald Delbert) |url=https://archive.org/details/principlesofstel0000clay/mode/2up |title=Principles of stellar evolution and nucleosynthesis: with a new preface |date=1983 |publisher=Chicago; London : University of Chicago Press |others=Internet Archive |isbn=978-0-226-10952-7}}</ref>
:<math>E_{\rm max}=\left[E_{\rm G}\left(\frac{k_{\rm B}T}{2}\right)^2\right]^{1/3}.</math>
This quantity is known as the Gamow peak.{{efn|At ''kT'' resp. ''E<sub>G</sub>'' the factors are 1/e (37%) at any temperature. Locus ''E<sub>0</sub>'' of the Gamow peak is <math display="inline">\propto T^{2/3}.</math>}}

Expanding <math>P_\text{fusion} </math> around <math>E_{\rm max} </math> gives:<ref name=":1" />
:<math>P_\text{fusion}(E)\approx P_\text{fusion}(E_\text{max})\cdot\left[1+\left(\frac{E-E_{\rm max}}{2\Delta}\right)^2+\cdots\right],</math> 
where (in joule) 
:<math>\Delta(T)=4\sqrt{\frac{E_{\rm max}k_{\rm B}T}{3}}=\frac{2^{5/3}}{\sqrt{3}}[E^{}_{\rm G}(k_{\rm B}T)^{5}]^{1/6}  </math>
is the Gamow window.{{efn|Double log. graphs <math>\Delta</math> vs T: <math>2\log(\Delta/4)=\log(k_{\rm B}T)+\log(E_{\rm max}/3)=[5\log(k_{\rm B}T)+\log(E_{\rm G})-3\log(3)-2\log(2)]/3</math>. Similar <math>\log(\Delta/4)=[5\log(k_{\rm B}T)+\log(E_{\rm G})-\log(27\cdot4)]/6</math>}}

== Derivation ==
[[File:Scanning tunneling microscope - rectangular potential barrier model.svg|thumb|300x300px|Top (black): Scheme of an energy barrier of height ''U'' as function of position. Bottom (red): Schrödinger wave-function with energy ''E.'']]

=== 1D problem ===
The derivation consists in the one-dimensional case of quantum tunnelling using the [[WKB approximation]].<ref>[http://web.ihep.su/dbserv/compas/src/gamow28/eng.pdf Quantum Theory of the Atomic Nucleus, G. Gamow]. Translated to English from: G. Gamow, ZP, 51, 204</ref> Considering a wave function of a particle of mass ''m'', we take area 1 to be where a wave is emitted, area 2 the potential barrier which has height ''V'' and width ''l'' (at <math display="inline">0<x<l</math>), and area 3 its other side, where the wave is arriving, partly transmitted and partly reflected. For wave numbers ''k'' [m<sup>−1</sup>] and energy ''E'' we get:
: <math>\Psi_1=Ae^{i(kx+\alpha)}e^{-i{Et}/{\hbar}}</math>
: <math>\Psi_2=B_1e^{-k'x}+B_2e^{k'x}</math>
: <math>\Psi_3=(C_1e^{-i(kx+\beta)}+C_2e^{i(kx+\beta')})\cdot e^{-i{Et}/{\hbar}}</math>
where <math>k = \sqrt{2mE/\hbar^2}</math> and <math display="inline">k' = \sqrt{2m(V-E)/\hbar^2},</math> both in [1/m]. This is solved for given ''A'' and phase ''&alpha;'' by taking the boundary conditions at the barrier edges, at <math>x=0</math> and <math>x=l</math>: there <math display="inline">\Psi_{1,3}(t)</math> and its derivatives must be equal on both sides. For <math>k'l \gg 1</math>, this is easily solved by ignoring the time exponential and considering the real part alone (the imaginary part has the same behaviour). We get, up to factors

* depending on the ''β'' phases which are typically of order 1, and 
* of the order of <math display="inline">{k}/{k'}=\sqrt{{E}/{(V-E)}}</math> (assumed not very large, since ''V'' is greater than ''E'' (not marginally)):
<math>\Psi_1=Ae^{i(kx+\alpha)} , \Psi_3=C_1e^{-i(kx+\beta)}+C_2e^{i(kx+\beta')},</math>

<math>\Psi_2\approx Ae^{-k'x} +Ae^{k'x}: B_1,B_2\approx A</math> and <math>C_1, C_2 \approx \frac{1}{2}A\frac{k'}{k} e^{k'l}.</math>

Next, the [[alpha decay]] can be modelled as a symmetric one-dimensional problem, with a standing wave between two symmetric potential barriers at <math>q_0<x<q_0+l</math> and <math>-(q_0+l)<x<-q_0</math>, and emitting waves at both outer sides of the barriers. Solving this can in principle be done by taking the solution of the first problem, translating it by <math>q_0</math> and gluing it to an identical solution reflected around <math>x=0</math>.
[[File:Potential-barrier-for-alpha-particle (simple).svg|thumb|Alpha decay modelled as two symmetrical Coulomb potential barriers in 1D.]]
Due to the symmetry of the problem, the emitting waves on both sides must have equal amplitudes (''A''), but their phases (''&alpha;'') may be different. This gives a single extra parameter; however, gluing the two solutions at <math display="inline">x=0</math> requires two boundary conditions (for both the wave function and its derivative), so in general there is no solution. In particular, re-writing <math display="inline">\Psi_3</math> (after translation by <math display="inline">q_0</math>) as a sum of a cosine and a sine of <math>kx</math>, each having a different factor that depends on ''k'' and ''β;'' the factor of the sine must vanish, so that the solution can be glued symmetrically to its reflection. Since the factor is in general complex (hence its vanishing imposes two constraints, representing the two boundary conditions), this can in general be solved by adding an imaginary part of ''k'', which gives the extra parameter needed. Thus ''E'' will have an imaginary part as well.

The physical meaning of this is that the [[standing wave]] in the middle decays; the waves newly emitted have therefore smaller amplitudes, so that their amplitude decays in time but grows with distance. The ''decay constant'', denoted ''&lambda;'' [1/s], is assumed small compared to <math display="inline">E/\hbar</math>.

''&lambda;'' can be estimated without solving explicitly, by noting its effect on the [[probability current]] [[conservation law]]. Since the probability flows from the middle to the sides, we have:
: <math> \frac {\partial}{\partial t} \int_{-(q_0+l)}^{(q_0+l)} \Psi^*\Psi\ dx = 2 \frac{\hbar}{2mi}\left(\Psi_1^* \frac{\partial \Psi_1 }{\partial x}- \Psi_1 \frac{\partial \Psi_1^* }{\partial x}  \right) ,</math>
note the factor of 2 is due to having two emitted waves.

Taking <math>\Psi\sim e^{-\lambda t}</math>, this gives:
: <math> \lambda\frac{2}{4} (q_0+l)\left(A\frac{k'}{k}\right)^2 e^{2k'l}\approx2\frac{\hbar}{m}A^2k.</math>
Since the quadratic dependence on <math>k'l</math> is negligible relative to its exponential dependence, we may write:
: <math> \lambda\approx4\frac{\hbar k}{m(q_0+l)} \frac{k^2}{k'^2}\cdot e^{-2k'l}. </math>
Remembering the imaginary part added to ''k'' is much smaller than the real part, we may now neglect it and get:
: <math> \lambda\approx4\frac{\hbar k}{m(q_0+l)}\cdot \frac{E}{V-E}\cdot e^{-2\sqrt{2m(V-E)}l/\hbar}. </math>
Note that <math display="inline">\frac{\hbar k}{m}=\sqrt{2E/m}</math> is the [[particle velocity]], so the first factor is the classical rate by which the particle trapped between the barriers (<math display="inline">2q_0</math> apart) hits them.

=== 3D problem ===
[[File:AlphaDecay.svg|thumb|300x300px|Scheme of the potential barrier in radial coordinates.]]

Finally, moving to the three-dimensional problem, the spherically symmetric [[Schrödinger equation]] reads (expanding the wave function <math>\psi(r,\theta,\phi) = \chi(r)u(\theta,\phi)</math> in [[spherical harmonics]] and looking at the ''l''-th term):
: <math>\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\left(\frac{d^2\chi}{dr^2}+\frac{2}{r}\frac{d\chi}{dr}\right)=\left(V(r)+\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{r^2}-E\right)\chi.</math>
Since <math>\ell>0</math> amounts to enlarging the potential, and therefore substantially reducing the [[Radioactive decay|decay rate]] (given its exponential dependence on <math display="inline">\sqrt{V-E}</math>): we focus on <math>\ell=0</math>, and get a very similar problem to the previous one with <math>\chi(r) = \Psi(r)/r </math>, except that now the potential as a function of ''r'' is not a [[step function]]. In short <math display="inline">\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\left(\ddot\chi+\frac{2}{r}\dot\chi\right)=\left(V(r)-E\right)\chi.</math>

The main effect of this on the amplitudes is that we must replace the argument in the exponent, taking an integral of <math display="inline"> 2\sqrt{2m(V-E)}/\hbar </math> over the distance where <math>V(r)>E</math> rather than multiplying by width ''l''. We take the [[Coulomb's law|Coulomb potential]]:
: <math> V(r) = \frac {z(Z-z) e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}</math>
where <math>\varepsilon_0</math> is the [[vacuum electric permittivity]], ''e'' the [[electron charge]], ''z'' = 2 is the [[charge number]] of the alpha particle and ''Z'' the charge number of the nucleus (''Z''–''z'' after emitting the particle). The integration limits are then:

<math>r_2 = \frac {z(Z-z) e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 E},</math> where we assume the nuclear [[potential energy]] is still relatively small, and

<math>r_1</math>, which is where the nuclear negative potential energy is large enough so that the overall potential is smaller than ''E''.

Thus, the argument of the exponent in ''&lambda;'' is:
: <math> 2\frac {\sqrt{2mE}}{\hbar}\int_{r_1}^{r_2}\sqrt{\frac{V(r)}{E}-1} \,dr=2\frac{\sqrt{2mE}}{\hbar}\int_{r_1}^{r_2}\sqrt{\frac{r_2}{r}-1}\,dr. </math>
This can be solved by substituting <math display="inline">t=\sqrt{r/r_2}</math> and then <math display="inline">t=\cos(\theta) </math> and solving for &theta;, giving:
: <math>2r_2\frac{\sqrt{2mE}}{\hbar}[\cos^{-1}(\sqrt{x})-\sqrt{x}\sqrt{1-x}]=2\frac{\sqrt{2m}z(Z-z)e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\hbar\sqrt{E}}\left[\cos^{-1}(\sqrt{x})-\sqrt{x}\sqrt{1-x}\right]</math>
where <math>x = r_1/r_2</math>. Since ''x'' is small, the ''x''-dependent factor is of the order 1.

Assuming <math display="inline">x\ll 1</math>, the ''x''-dependent factor can be replaced by <math display="inline">\arccos0=\pi/2,</math> giving:<blockquote><math>\lambda\approx e^{-\sqrt{{E_{\mathrm{G}}}/{E}}}</math> with <math>E_{\mathrm G}=\frac{2\pi^2m\left[z(Z-z)e^2\right]^2}{(4\pi\varepsilon_0\hbar)^2}.</math></blockquote>Which is the same as the formula given in the beginning of the article with <math display="inline">Z_\text{a}=z</math>, <math display="inline">Z_\text{b}=Z-z</math> and the fine-structure constant <math display="inline">\alpha=\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\hbar c}: \sqrt{E_{\rm G}}=\sqrt{2m}/(4\epsilon_0\hbar)[Z_aeZ_be].</math>

For a [[radium]] alpha decay, ''Z'' = 88, ''z'' = 2 and ''m'' ≈ 4[[proton mass|''m''<sub>p</sub>]], ''E''<sub>G</sub> is approximately 50&nbsp;[[GeV]]. Gamow calculated the slope of <math display="inline">\log(\lambda)</math> with respect to ''E'' at an energy of 5&nbsp;[[MeV]] to be ~&nbsp;10<sup>14</sup>&nbsp;J<sup>−1</sup>, compared to the experimental value of {{val|0.7|e=14|u=J<sup>−1</sup>}}.{{efn|1=<math display="inline">\log\lambda\approx-100</math>; <math display="inline">{\operatorname{d}\log\lambda\over\operatorname{d}\!E}=\tfrac{1}{2}E_{\rm G}^{1/2}/E^{3/2}</math> (Natural log.)
Around 10 /MeV; 'kT = 0.217 fJ = 0.135 keV', 'typical core temperatures in main-sequence stars (the Sun) give kT of the order of 1 keV': <math display="inline">2.17\times10^{-16}</math> joule}}

== History ==
In 1927, [[Ernest Rutherford]] published an article in ''[[Philosophical Magazine]]'' on a problem related to [[Hans Geiger]]'s 1921 experiment of scattering [[alpha particle]]s from [[uranium]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Merzbacher |first=Eugen |date=2002-08-01 |title=The Early History of Quantum Tunneling |url=https://pubs.aip.org/physicstoday/article-abstract/55/8/44/412308/The-Early-History-of-Quantum-Tunneling-Molecular?redirectedFrom=fulltext |journal=Physics Today |volume=55 |issue=8 |pages=44–49 |doi=10.1063/1.1510281 |bibcode=2002PhT....55h..44M |issn=0031-9228|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Previous experiments with thorium C' (now called [[polonium]]-262){{efn|<sub>88</sub>Ra (<sub>90</sub>Th) <sub>92</sub>U are radioactive elements in periods 7, <sub>84</sub>Po in period 6. Spontaneous nuclear fission}} confirmed that uranium has a Coulomb barrier of 8.57 MeV, however uranium emitted alpha particles of 4.2 MeV.<ref name=":0" /> The emitted energy was too low to overcome the barrier. On 29 July 1928, George Gamow, and independently the next day [[Ronald Wilfred Gurney]] and [[Edward Condon]] submitted their solution based on quantum tunnelling to the journal ''[[Zeitschrift für Physik]]''.<ref name=":0" /> Their work was based on previous work on tunnelling by [[J. Robert Oppenheimer]], [[Gregor Wentzel]], [[Lothar Wolfgang Nordheim]], and [[Ralph H. Fowler]].<ref name=":0" /> Gurney and Condon cited also [[Friedrich Hund]].<ref name=":0" />

In 1931, [[Arnold Sommerfeld]] introduced a similar factor (a [[Gaunt factor]]) for the discussion of [[bremsstrahlung]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Iben |first=Icko |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hFmpIXwLUvIC&dq=sommerfeld++1931+factor&pg=PA335 |title=Stellar Evolution Physics |date=2013 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-107-01656-9 |language=en}}</ref>

Gamow popularized his personal version of the discovery in his 1970's book, ''My World Line: An Informal Autobiography.<ref name=":0" />''
